source_title: Unlawful use of unmanned aircraft over open-air facility / critical infrastructure
effective_date: Aug. 28, 2020 (orig.); amended by HB 2637, effective June 12, 2026 (emergency clause)
uas_topic: Open-air facility and critical-infrastructure UAS restriction
regulated_activity: Flight below 400 ft AGL within the property line of an open-air facility or critical infrastructure facility; delivery of prohibited items
summary: As codified through 2020 (last text independently verified), §577.800 makes it an infraction to purposely operate a UAS within 400 ft AGL and within the property line of an 'open-air facility' (sports/theater/music/entertainment venue, previously defined as capacity 5,000+), or to use a UAS to deliver a weapon (Class B felony) or controlled substance (Class D felony) to a person there. Exemptions include facility-authorized operators, law enforcement/fire/EMS and government employees on official duty, and public utilities/rural electric cooperatives inspecting/maintaining utility infrastructure (with advance notice to the facility). HB 2637, signed June 12, 2026 with an emergency effective clause (enacted ahead of Kansas City's 2026 FIFA World Cup matches), is reported to lower the open-air facility capacity threshold from 5,000 to 500, extend the restriction to a new 'critical infrastructure facility' category (e.g., water, wastewater, and electric power plants), and add explosive-device delivery as a Class B felony.
practical_interpretation_aec_expert: Treat any event venue with 500+ capacity and any water/wastewater/power facility as inside the 400 ft AGL restricted zone by default for Missouri work scheduled from mid-2026 forward — the lowered threshold sweeps in far more venues than the pre-2026 rule, so re-check any standing Missouri site list built before the amendment. For utility inspection work, give the facility advance notice as required by the utility exemption rather than assuming the exemption is self-executing.
practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: The codified text pulled directly from the Revisor of Statutes site during this research still shows the pre-amendment (5,000-person, no critical-infrastructure) version, which may reflect a lag in the site's update following the June 2026 emergency-clause enactment — confirm the current codified text directly before citing a specific threshold or definition in a client-facing document. Document the specific exemption relied upon (utility inspection, government duty, facility consent) for any flight near a covered venue or facility given the felony-level exposure for prohibited deliveries.
verification_status: Pre-2026 text verified directly against Revisor of Statutes; 2026 HB 2637 amendments confirmed via multiple secondary press/legal sources (StateScoop, KFVS12, Jefferson City News-Tribune) but not yet independently re-verified against updated codified text, which had not visibly updated on revisor.mo.gov as of the date accessed
notes: High-priority re-verification item: pull the current revisor.mo.gov text again closer to project execution to confirm the exact amended threshold, critical-infrastructure definition, and any new exemptions.

source_title: Correctional center, unlawful use of unmanned aircraft over
regulated_activity: Operating a UAS within 400 ft over a correctional center's secure perimeter fence, or allowing contact with the facility
summary: Makes it an offense to purposely operate a UAS within a vertical distance of 400 ft over a correctional center's secure perimeter fence, or to allow a UAS to make contact with the facility (including any person or object on the premises). 'Correctional center' is defined broadly to include state correctional centers (§217.010), private jails (§221.095), and county or municipal jails. Exemptions include facility-authorized operators, written consent from the chief administrative officer, law enforcement/fire/EMS and government employees on official duty, and qualifying public utility/rural electric cooperative infrastructure work.
practical_interpretation_aec_expert: Identify any state, private, county, or municipal correctional/jail facility near a project site during pre-flight planning and maintain the 400 ft vertical standoff by default unless the project specifically requires facility work, in which case get the chief administrative officer's written consent first.
practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: Retain written consent documentation for any flight authorized near a correctional facility; the broad definition of 'correctional center' (reaching county and municipal jails, not just state prisons) means this statute applies more often than a quick check for 'state prison' alone would suggest.
verification_status: Statute text and structure confirmed via direct citation and cross-checked secondary summary; recommend a direct revisor.mo.gov pull for exact current wording before final client use

source_title: 'Preserving Freedom from Unwarranted Surveillance Act' — NOT current law
citation: Proposed as RSMo 305.635–305.641 (HB 46 in 2013; HB 1204; HB 209 in 2025) — these section numbers do not exist in current Missouri statutes
source_type: Repealed, expired, or superseded authority (never enacted)
status: Not law - reintroduced multiple sessions (2013, later sessions, 2025) without passing
uas_topic: Myth-busting: general drone surveillance-consent statute claim
requirement_type: N/A - widely repeated as if current law
commercial_operator_relevance: High (risk of relying on bad information)
aec_relevance: High (risk of relying on bad information)
summary: A bill titled the 'Preserving Freedom from Unwarranted Surveillance Act' would prohibit any person, entity, or state agency from using a drone to conduct surveillance or observation of an individual, their property, a farm, or agricultural industry without consent (absent a warrant). It has been introduced repeatedly since 2013 (HB 46, HB 1204, HB 209 in 2025) and has never passed. Some secondary sources describe or cite this as if it were current Missouri law; it is not.
practical_interpretation_aec_expert: Do not build a general Missouri drone-surveillance-consent or farm/agricultural-consent step into standard operating procedure based on this bill — it is not currently required by Missouri statute. Rely on the actual enacted statutes (open-air facility, correctional center) and ordinary privacy/trespass considerations instead.
practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: Correct this specific point if it appears in any internal compliance document or client-facing guidance sourced from a drone-law aggregator; Missouri currently has no comprehensive UAS privacy/surveillance-consent statute analogous to those in some other states, which is itself a notable gap worth flagging to the client rather than asserting a nonexistent consent requirement.
verification_status: Bill history (2013 HB46, HB1204, 2025 HB209) and repeated failure-to-pass confirmed via secondary legal-summary source; recommend independently confirming current-session bill status directly at house.mo.gov before relying on this for a specific client date
notes: Retained as an explicit myth-busting record given how easily a bill title like this could be mistaken for enacted law by someone skimming a secondary source.

source_title: Unmanned Aerial Systems Security Act of 2025 — did not pass
source_type: Proposed or pending authority (died in committee)
regulated_party: Would have applied to Missouri government agencies
regulated_activity: Government purchase/use of UAS from manufacturers domiciled in a 'country of concern'
summary: HB 210 would have prohibited Missouri government agencies from purchasing or using a UAS (or related services/equipment) from a manufacturer domiciled in a designated 'country of concern' (China, Russia, Iran, North Korea, Cuba, Venezuela's Maduro regime, or Syria, with the governor able to expand the list), required federally compliant encryption for drone communications, established a three-tier drone classification system, and included a Department of Public Safety replacement-grant program for affected agencies. The bill drew opposition from law enforcement and died in committee on May 16, 2025; it was not enacted.
practical_interpretation_aec_expert: No Missouri state procurement restriction currently limits fleet/manufacturer choice for private commercial work or for public-agency contract work, but track whether this bill (or a successor) is reintroduced in a future session, since similar bills have passed in other states.
practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: Do not represent to a client that Missouri has (or is about to have) a manufacturer-restriction law based on this bill; it failed and there is no guarantee a successor will pass. Separately confirm the federal American Security Drone Act / OMB M-26-02 restrictions (see MO-006) for any federally funded engagement, since those apply regardless of state law.
verification_status: Bill status ('Dead,' died 5/16/2025) confirmed via secondary bill-tracking source; not independently re-confirmed against house.mo.gov/senate.mo.gov bill-tracking pages in this pass

source_title: New Federal Restrictions on Foreign Drones (effective Dec. 22, 2025) — MoDOT notice
citation: MoDOT agency notice implementing the American Security Drone Act of 2023 (ASDA) and OMB Memorandum M-26-02 (federal authority, not Missouri state law)
source_type: Official agency policy (state agency notice of federal requirement)
binding_level: Binding at the federal level for federally funded UAS procurement/use; MoDOT notice is informational/administrative for its own program and contractors
uas_topic: Federally funded UAS procurement restriction (foreign-manufacturer ban)
regulated_party: Entities using federal funds for UAS, including MoDOT and its contractors on federally funded projects
regulated_activity: Procurement/use of UAS (including components: flight controller, camera, ground control station) from a covered foreign entity, specifically manufacturers based in or controlled by the People's Republic of China
requirement_type: Procurement prohibition (federal, administered through MoDOT for its programs)
permit_or_approval_required: No permit; compliance is an equipment-sourcing requirement
public_agency_only: No - applies to any recipient of the federal funds in question, which can include consultants on federally funded MoDOT contracts
commercial_operator_relevance: High for federally funded transportation work
aec_relevance: High for federally funded transportation work
summary: MoDOT published a notice explaining that, effective December 22, 2025, the federal American Security Drone Act of 2023 and OMB Memorandum M-26-02 prohibit the use of federal funds for UAS manufactured by 'covered foreign entities,' including any aircraft, flight controller, camera, or ground control station from a manufacturer based in or controlled by the People's Republic of China (and other designated foreign adversary countries). This is a federal requirement; MoDOT's notice serves to inform its programs and contractors of the obligation as it flows down through federally funded transportation work.
practical_interpretation_aec_expert: If your firm does UAS work on any federally funded MoDOT (or other Missouri agency) transportation project, audit your fleet against covered-foreign-entity status before mobilizing — this is a hard equipment-sourcing constraint, not a preference, and it applies at the component level (flight controller, camera, ground station), not just the airframe brand.
practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: Confirm whether a specific MoDOT task order is federally funded (versus 100% state-funded) before assuming ASDA/OMB M-26-02 applies, since the restriction is tied to the federal-funds nexus rather than being a general Missouri state law; document equipment compliance representations in the proposal for any federally funded scope.
verification_status: Verified directly from MoDOT's own published notice
notes: Federal-origin requirement administered through a Missouri state agency; included because it materially affects commercial AEC UAS operations on Missouri DOT-funded work.

citation: MDC conservation area regulations (special use permit); Wildlife Code of Missouri, 3 CSR 10-7.410 and related rules
source_type: Binding administrative regulation + Official agency policy
effective_date: Current (2024 rule update reported for game-recovery provision)
uas_topic: Conservation-area launch/landing restriction; wildlife harassment; hunting-related drone use
regulated_party: UAS operators on MDC conservation areas; hunters
regulated_activity: Launching/landing/operating a UAS on an MDC conservation area; using a UAS to pursue, take, drive, or harass wildlife; drone-assisted game recovery
requirement_type: Permit requirement (launch/land) + prohibition (wildlife harassment) with a narrow permitted exception (game recovery)
permit_or_approval_required: Yes - MDC special use permit required to launch, land, or operate a UAS on a conservation area (except conservation-agent-authorized wounded-game recovery)
summary: MDC requires a special use permit to launch, land, or operate a UAS on any of its 1,000+ conservation areas statewide. Separately, the Wildlife Code of Missouri (3 CSR 10-7.410 and related rules) forbids using a UAS to pursue, take, drive, or molest wildlife, or to operate it in a way that harasses wildlife or other visitors, with a narrow exception (added in a recent rule update) allowing drone-assisted recovery of wounded deer, turkey, elk, or black bear during the applicable season, with landowner permission and prior conservation-agent authorization, and no weapon on the operator.
practical_interpretation_aec_expert: Treat any MDC conservation area the same as a state park for launch/landing purposes - apply for the special use permit before staging a crew there for environmental monitoring, habitat mapping, or resource-inventory work, and build the permit lead time into project scheduling.
practical_interpretation_legal_counsel: Retain the MDC special use permit in the project file for any conservation-area launch/land activity; document flight altitude and purpose for work near wildlife concentrations, since the harassment standard in the Wildlife Code is judgment-based similarly to other states' wildlife-harassment rules.
verification_status: Special use permit requirement and Wildlife Code citation confirmed via MDC's own webpage and secondary legal-summary sources; full 3 CSR 10-7.410 text not independently pulled and re-parsed in this pass
notes: Recommend pulling the current 3 CSR 10-7.410 text directly from the Missouri Code of State Regulations before finalizing conservation-area flight protocols.
